title: forallx: An Introduction to Formal Logic — Chapters 1–15
source: User-provided forallx Intro to Formal Logic PDF

cards.prompt: What would show that an argument is invalid?
options: A case where every premise is true and the conclusion is false
A case where one premise and the conclusion are both false
A case where the conclusion is true
A case where the premises are jointly false
cards.answer: A counterexample: all premises true and the conclusion false.
cards.elaboration: Validity rules out that combination; one such case is enough to refute validity.

cards.prompt: Which description correctly defines a sound argument?
options: It is valid and has true premises
It has a true conclusion
It has at least one true premise
It is invalid but persuasive
cards.answer: A sound argument is valid and all of its premises are true.
cards.elaboration: A sound argument guarantees a true conclusion because validity preserves truth from true premises.

cards.prompt: A sentence is logically necessary when…
options: it is true in every possible circumstance
it is true in the actual world only
it follows from one particular argument
it contains a logical connective
cards.answer: It is true in every possible circumstance.
cards.elaboration: Logical necessity concerns all possibilities, not merely what happens to be true here and now.

cards.prompt: When are a set of premises jointly possible?
options: When there is at least one possible circumstance in which all are true
When each premise is true in a different circumstance
When their conclusion is necessarily true
When at least one premise is false
cards.answer: When some possible circumstance makes every premise true together.
cards.elaboration: Joint possibility asks whether the premises can all be true at once.

cards.prompt: What does it mean for premises Γ to entail a conclusion C?
options: There is no possible case where every member of Γ is true and C is false
C is grammatically shorter than every premise
Γ and C are both true in the actual world
C is true whenever any one premise is true
cards.answer: Γ entails C exactly when no possible case makes all the premises true and C false.
cards.elaboration: Entailment is the premise-to-conclusion relation expressed by validity.

cards.prompt: Two sentences are logically equivalent when…
options: they have the same truth value in every possible circumstance
they use the same words
they are both true in the actual world
each entails the other only in one selected case
cards.answer: They match in truth value in every possible circumstance.
cards.elaboration: Equivalence can be checked by testing whether either sentence can be true while the other is false.

cards.prompt: What is the job of a symbolization key?
options: It states which English sentence each sentence letter represents
It lists the truth values assigned to every sentence
It defines the argument's conclusion
It removes ambiguity by changing the English wording
cards.answer: A key pairs sentence letters with the English sentences they stand for.
cards.elaboration: The key lets a reader interpret the symbolic form without guessing what its letters mean.

cards.prompt: An argument is valid in virtue of its form when…
options: every interpretation of its sentence letters preserves truth from premises to conclusion
its premises happen to be true in the actual world
its conclusion repeats a word from a premise
the argument contains at least one conditional
cards.answer: Its logical pattern guarantees that true premises cannot accompany a false conclusion, regardless of the sentence-letter meanings.
cards.elaboration: Symbolization makes the shared logical structure visible while abstracting from topic-specific content.

cards.prompt: Which TFL connective best represents ‘neither P nor Q’?
options: P ∨ Q
P → Q
P ↔ Q
cards.elaboration: ‘Neither’ denies that at least one of the two disjuncts is true.

cards.prompt: In standard TFL, what does P ∨ Q require to be true?
options: At least one of P or Q is true, including the case where both are true
Exactly one of P and Q is true
Both P and Q are true
If P is true, then Q is true
cards.answer: At least one disjunct is true; both may be true as well.
cards.elaboration: TFL’s disjunction is inclusive, unlike an exclusive ‘either-or’ reading.

cards.prompt: Which expression is a well-formed compound sentence of TFL?
options: (P ∧ Q)
P ∧
(P Q)
→ P Q
cards.elaboration: A binary connective joins two sentences, and the parentheses mark the resulting structure.

cards.prompt: What is the main connective in ¬(P ∧ Q)?
options: The outer negation ¬
The conjunction ∧
P
Q
cards.answer: The outer negation is the main connective.
cards.elaboration: The main connective is the operator introduced last in the sentence’s construction and governs the whole expression.

cards.prompt: What kind of ambiguity occurs when the same words allow different grammatical groupings?
options: Structural ambiguity
Lexical ambiguity
Truth-functional ambiguity
A symbolization key
cards.answer: Structural ambiguity.
cards.elaboration: Different groupings can correspond to different scopes for connectives, even if the words stay the same.

cards.prompt: Why might ‘not both P and Q’ differ from ‘neither P nor Q’?
options: The first can allow one of P or Q to be true; the second requires both false
They always have exactly the same meaning
The first is a conditional and the second is a biconditional
Neither sentence can be represented in TFL
cards.answer: ‘Not both’ is ¬(P ∧ Q); ‘neither’ is ¬P ∧ ¬Q, so exactly one may be true in the first but not the second.
cards.elaboration: Scope and grouping determine whether negation applies to a conjunction or separately to both parts.

cards.prompt: In logic, what is the use/mention distinction?
options: Using an expression to talk about its subject versus mentioning the expression itself
Using a connective versus omitting it
Writing a sentence versus assigning it a truth value
Using a premise versus citing a conclusion
cards.answer: Using a word or sentence to talk about what it means differs from mentioning that expression as an object of discussion.
cards.elaboration: Quotation marks commonly signal mention, as in discussing the word ‘and’ itself.

cards.prompt: In the sentence ‘“P ∧ Q” contains a connective,’ what is being discussed?
options: The written symbolic expression itself
The truth of P and Q in the world
An argument with P and Q as premises
The connective’s English pronunciation only
cards.answer: The expression ‘P ∧ Q’ is mentioned; the sentence is about the notation itself.
cards.elaboration: Quotation marks help distinguish an expression from the sentence it would represent.

cards.prompt: On what row is a material conditional P → Q false?
options: P is true and Q is false
P is false and Q is true
Both P and Q are true
Both P and Q are false
cards.answer: Only when P is true and Q is false.
cards.elaboration: A conditional rules out a true antecedent paired with a false consequent.

cards.prompt: When is the biconditional P ↔ Q true?
options: When P and Q have the same truth value
Only when P is true
Only when Q is false
Whenever at least one of P or Q is true
cards.answer: When both sides are true or both sides are false.
cards.elaboration: The biconditional is true exactly when its component sentences agree in truth value.

cards.prompt: A connective is truth-functional when…
options: the truth value of the compound is determined entirely by the truth values of its parts
its English use always indicates a causal relation
it can only join true sentences
its meaning depends on the topic of the sentence
cards.answer: The compound’s truth value depends only on the truth values of its component sentences.
cards.elaboration: Truth-functional semantics intentionally ignores extra conversational or causal meaning.

cards.prompt: Which statement about TFL’s five standard connectives is correct?
options: Each has a truth rule that applies to every sentence with that connective
Their truth values depend on whether the sentence is about people
Only negation has a truth table
Their English translations always have one unambiguous reading
cards.answer: Each connective receives a uniform truth-functional rule.
cards.elaboration: Once the component truth values are fixed, the connective’s table determines the compound’s value.

cards.prompt: How many rows are in a complete truth table with four distinct sentence letters?
cards.answer: 16 rows, since 2⁴ = 16.
cards.elaboration: Each of four sentence letters can be true or false, producing every combination.

cards.prompt: What does each row of a complete truth table represent?
options: One assignment of truth values to all sentence letters
One premise paired with the conclusion
One possible English translation
One connective’s definition
cards.answer: A single valuation assigning T or F to every sentence letter.
cards.elaboration: A complete table includes every valuation for the letters in the sentence or argument.

cards.prompt: Which column pattern makes a sentence a tautology?
options: True on every valuation
False on every valuation
True on one row only
Missing a value on at least one row
cards.answer: A tautology is true on every valuation.
cards.elaboration: A contradiction is false on every valuation; a contingent sentence varies across rows.

cards.prompt: How can a truth table show that Γ does not entail C?
options: Find a row where every premise is true and C is false
Find a row where every premise and C are false
Find a row where C is true
Find any row where a premise is false
cards.answer: A valuation with all premises true and the conclusion false is a counterexample to entailment.
cards.elaboration: Validity and entailment fail as soon as one such row appears.

cards.prompt: What important structure does TFL normally treat as a single sentence letter?
options: The internal subject-and-predicate structure of an atomic sentence
The truth table for negation
The main connective of a compound
The order of the argument’s premises
cards.answer: TFL treats an atomic sentence as an unanalyzed unit, represented by one sentence letter.
cards.elaboration: This abstraction makes TFL useful for connective patterns but limits what it can express about internal sentence structure.

cards.prompt: Why can’t ordinary TFL directly express ‘Everyone admires someone’?
options: It lacks quantifiers and a way to represent relations among individuals
It has no symbol for negation
It cannot use sentence letters
It cannot represent any compound sentence
cards.answer: TFL has no quantifier or predicate-and-variable machinery for representing people and their relations.
cards.elaboration: A richer system such as predicate logic is needed to expose that internal structure.

cards.prompt: If P is false, what can you conclude about P ∧ Q without evaluating Q?
options: P ∧ Q is false
P ∧ Q is true
P ∧ Q has no truth value
Nothing; Q must be evaluated first
cards.answer: The conjunction is false regardless of Q.
cards.elaboration: This is a truth-table shortcut: one false conjunct settles the whole conjunction.

cards.prompt: If P is true, what can you conclude about P ∨ Q without evaluating Q?
options: P ∨ Q is true
P ∨ Q is false
P ∨ Q is equivalent to Q
P ∨ Q is contingent
cards.answer: The disjunction is true regardless of Q.
cards.elaboration: One true disjunct is enough for an inclusive disjunction to be true.

cards.prompt: What can one row of a partial truth table establish about an argument?
options: A row with all premises true and the conclusion false establishes invalidity
A row with all premises true establishes validity
A row with a false premise establishes invalidity
A row with a true conclusion establishes validity
cards.answer: A counterexample row establishes that the argument is invalid.
cards.elaboration: Disproof needs only one failing valuation, so a partial table can be decisive.

cards.prompt: Why can a partial truth table usually not prove that a sentence is a tautology?
options: A proof must establish truth on every valuation, including rows not yet checked
Partial tables cannot assign truth values
A tautology must be true on exactly one row
Truth tables only evaluate arguments, not sentences
cards.answer: A tautology requires truth on all valuations, so unexamined rows still need to be ruled out.
cards.elaboration: Partial tables are especially useful for finding a counterexample, where one row is enough.
